context: The travelers reach the second of the seven terraces, where envy is purged.

note: The mountain narrows as it rises, so each terrace is a smaller circle than the one below.

Dante's Italian says no "ombra" is to be seen, a word that means both a shade, one of the dead, and a figure or image. The terrace looks empty: no souls in sight and, unlike the terrace of pride, no sculptures. The souls here are blind, and pictures would be wasted on them.
The Italian word is "livido", the blue-gray of a bruise. It was the traditional color of envy, as in the English "livid".

quote: his eyes steadily on the sun
note: It is just past noon. With no one to ask, Virgil takes the sun as guide and turns to the right, the direction the travelers keep on every terrace.
Virgil's prayer to the sun. The sun often stands for God in the poem, but Virgil, a pagan, speaks of it as the light of the natural world, the best guide he has unless a higher one is given.
The examples of virtue on this terrace come as voices in the air, not carvings, because the souls here cannot see. The speakers are never identified.
The virtue opposed to envy is charity: love of others and gladness at their good. The voices invite the souls to its table.

The Virgin Mary's words at the wedding at Cana (John 2:3). She noticed the hosts' embarrassment and asked her son to help, and he turned water into wine. On every terrace the first example of the virtue is taken from her life.

A classical example of friendship. When Orestes was condemned to death, his friend Pylades claimed to be Orestes so as to die in his place, while Orestes insisted on who he was. Dante knew the story from Cicero's book on friendship.

quote: Love those who have wronged you!
note: Christ's command in the Sermon on the Mount: "Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you" (Matthew 5:44).

Virgil gives the method of every terrace. The whip is the set of examples of the virtue, which drive the souls forward. The bridle is the set of examples of the sin punished, which hold them back from it.
Not a gate: Dante's Italian says "the pass of pardon". It is the stair up to the next terrace, where an angel wipes away the mark of envy. The bridle is heard at the end of Canto 14.

quote: no different in color from the stone
note: The souls wear the bruise-gray of envy and can hardly be told from the rock. In life they could not bear to see others stand out.

context: The souls are chanting the Litany of the Saints, a long prayer that calls on Mary, the angels and the saints one by one, with the answer "pray for us".

quote: Michael and Peter and all Saints
note: More of the litany: the archangel Michael, the apostle Peter, and at the end all the saints together. The envious resented other people's good. Now they ask others for help and wish them glory.
Haircloth, rough and scratchy, the dress of penitents.
In life each wanted the others to fall. Here they prop one another up.
Dante's Italian says they beg "at the pardons": the feast days when indulgences were offered and crowds came to church, so that beggars gathered at the doors.
The penance fits the sin. The Latin word for envy, invidia, comes from a verb for looking askance at someone. Eyes that could not bear the sight of another's happiness are sewn shut.
Falconers tamed a newly caught hawk by stitching its eyelids closed with thread for a time, so that it would grow used to being handled.
A point of courtesy. To stare at people who cannot look back feels to Dante like taking advantage of them.
Dante himself. Virgil reads his thought before he asks.
God. Dante opens with the promise that matters most to the blind: they are certain to see, and to see the greatest sight there is.
A hard phrase. It is usually read as memory or thought, which will run clear once the film of sin is gone from the conscience.

The city of God, Heaven. The soul gently corrects Dante's question: no one here is Italian any more. On earth everyone is a traveler passing through, an idea from the New Testament (Hebrews 13:14) that Saint Augustine built into his City of God. Envy fed on local rivalries, and this soul has put them behind her.
A detail taken from life: a blind person listening for someone tilts the face up toward the voice.
A play on her name. Sapia sounds like "savia", the Italian for wise.

context: She was the aunt of Provenzan Salvani, the Sienese leader met among the proud in Canto 11. The battle she describes is the one in which he was killed.

note: Dante pictured a life as an arch that rises to its top at thirty-five and then comes down. She was past the middle of life, old enough to know better.

Colle di Val d'Elsa, a town between Siena and Florence. In June 1269 the Florentine Guelphs and their French allies routed the Sienese Ghibellines there. Why Sapia hated her own city's side is not known: perhaps envy of her nephew's power.
She prayed for her own people's defeat. God had already willed it for his own reasons, so her prayer changed nothing, but the wish was hers.
An old Italian folk tale. After a few mild days at the end of January, the blackbird thinks winter is over and sings, "Lord, I fear you no more." Then the cold comes back.
Like Provenzan Salvani, she repented late and should still be waiting outside the gate of Purgatory. Like him, she was let in early, in her case through another person's prayers.
Peter the comb-seller, a shopkeeper of Siena known for his scrupulous honesty and holy life, linked to the Franciscans. He died in 1289 and the city honored him as a saint.
She cannot see that Dante is alive, but she hears him breathe as he talks, which shades do not do.

quote: will yet be taken from me
note: Dante judges himself. After death he expects a short stay here, with his eyes sewn like theirs, since he has envied little.
The stones of the terrace of pride. Pride is the sin Dante knows to be his own, and he expects a long time under that weight.
Virgil, who keeps silent through the whole meeting. Dante does not name him.
The usual offer to souls in Purgatory: back on earth, Dante can go to their relatives and ask for the prayers that shorten their time.
Her family may believe she is damned. If they learn she is saved, they will remember her kindly and pray for her.
The Sienese. Their vanity was a standing joke in Florence, and Dante makes it again in Inferno 29. Sapia has left envy behind, but she still has a sharp tongue for her fellow citizens.

A small port on the Tuscan coast, bought by Siena in 1303 in the hope of becoming a sea power like Genoa and Pisa. The harbor kept silting up and the place was unhealthy with malaria. The scheme came to nothing.
An underground river that the Sienese believed ran beneath their hilltop city, which was always short of water. They spent large sums digging for it and never found it.
The meaning is disputed. They may be the men who hoped to command Siena's fleet, or the officials and contractors sent to work on the harbor, many of whom are said to have died of fever there.
